passages.t: ‘He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High’
passages.happening:
Psalm 91 has no heading. It begins with a sentence anyone can hear: “He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High will abide in the shadow of the Almighty” (verse 1). Then a voice answers for itself: “I will say to the LORD, ‘You are my refuge and my fortress, my God, in whom I trust’” (verse 2).

From verse 3 the psalm speaks to ‘you’. God will save you from the hunter's trap and from deadly plague (verse 3). “He will cover you with His feathers; under His wings you will find refuge; His faithfulness is a shield and rampart” (verse 4).

It names fears at every hour. “You will not fear the terror of the night, nor the arrow that flies by day, nor the pestilence that stalks in the darkness, nor the calamity that destroys at noon” (verses 5 to 6).

Then the boldest words. “Though a thousand may fall at your side, and ten thousand at your right hand, no harm will come near you” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
The dangers were real to the first hearers. A bird-catcher, the ‘fowler’, set hidden nets and snares. Plague swept through towns, and no one knew its cause or cure. Lions and cobras lived in the land. Many of Israel's neighbours met these fears with many gods and many charms. Psalm 91 meets them with one refuge, called by four names in two verses: the Most High, the Almighty, the LORD, my God.

The picture of wings is a mother bird sheltering her young. Moses' song pictures God like an eagle that “spread His wings to catch them and carried them on His pinions” (Deuteronomy 32:11).

Psalm 91 comes right after Psalm 90, which counted how short a life is. Psalm 90 began, ‘Lord, You have been our dwelling place’. Psalm 91 picks up the same Hebrew word: ‘Because you have made the LORD your dwelling’ (verse 9). Whoever arranged the Psalms set a song of refuge right after a song about death. The book is not naive about dying.

The habit of praying this psalm is old. The Rule of Saint Benedict, written for monks, has them sing it every night at Compline, the last prayer before sleep.
passages.later:
Jesus used the same picture of wings when he grieved over Jerusalem: “how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings” (Matthew 23:37).

He told his followers that they would be hated and some would die, and then said, “Yet not even a hair of your head will perish” (Luke 21:18). Both sentences are his. Only the hope of resurrection lets both be true.
passages.hard:
Faithful people do die of plague and fall in war. How can verse 7 say no harm will come near? If the psalm were a guarantee that believers are never hurt, it would have failed many times over, and it is honest to say so. The site's page on Psalm 91 in context, ‘Does Psalm 91 Promise Protection From Harm?’, takes up this question at length, and these notes agree with it.

The psalm is poetry of trust. It tells the truth about where a life held by God is going and where it ends. It is not a contract against every wound. Its own last verses say, ‘I will be with him in trouble’ (verse 15), which means trouble will come.

So this psalm is never a reason to refuse a doctor, medicine, or the ordinary care God also gives. Praying it and taking the medicine belong together.
passages.asks:
Pray this psalm for real dangers: the surgery, the night shift, the child with a fever, the long drive. It invites that.

But pray it as trust, not as a charm. The shelter in verse 1 is not a lucky word. It is a person. The shield in verse 4 is God's faithfulness, not the strength of your prayer.

passages.t: ‘He will command His angels concerning you’, and the tempter's reading
passages.happening:
The promises go on. Because you have made the LORD your dwelling, the psalm says, “no evil will befall you, no plague will approach your tent” (verse 10).

Then angels. “For He will command His angels concerning you to guard you in all your ways” (verse 11). “They will lift you up in their hands, so that you will not strike your foot against a stone” (verse 12).

“You will tread on the lion and cobra; you will trample the young lion and serpent” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
‘In all your ways’ (verse 11) matters. A ‘way’ is a road, the path of a life lived with God. The angels guard the traveller on the road God gives. They are not a net for someone who jumps off a cliff to prove a point.

The lion and the cobra were the most feared animals in the land, one by its strength, the other by its hidden bite. The psalm pictures the one who trusts God walking safely past both.

Notice that verse 10 says ‘no plague will approach your tent’. A tent was a home. The promise covers ordinary life at home, not only the battlefield.
passages.later:
This is the only psalm the devil quotes in the Gospels. He took Jesus to the highest point of the temple and told him to throw himself down. Then he quoted the psalm: “He will command His angels concerning You, and they will lift You up in their hands, so that You will not strike Your foot against a stone” (Matthew 4:6). Luke tells the same scene, with the quotation in Luke 4:10-11.

He quoted it accurately but selectively. In neither Gospel does he say ‘in all your ways’. The psalm promised a guard along the road God gives. The devil proposed a leap.

Jesus refused. He replied, “It is also written: ‘Do not put the Lord your God to the test.’” (Matthew 4:7). That command comes from Deuteronomy 6:16, which remembers Massah, where Israel demanded water and asked, “Is the LORD among us or not?” (Exodus 17:7).
passages.hard:
Jesus' refusal settles how this psalm may be used. To test God is to make him prove himself on our terms. So Psalm 91 is not a promise that no believer is ever harmed. And it is never a reason to refuse medical care, to skip ordinary caution, or to run a risk in order to test God. Jesus would not do that with this very psalm. Neither should we.

If you have prayed this psalm over someone you have since lost, you did not pray wrong, and the one you lost was not loved less. In one chapter of Acts, “He had James, the brother of John, put to death with the sword” (Acts 12:2), while Peter was set free from prison. Acts never says that James had less faith. The context page on Psalm 91 says more about this.
passages.asks:
Ask yourself how you use God's promises. Do you use them to rest in God, or to try to make him do what you want? Jesus shows the difference. He trusted his Father, and he would not test him.

Where are you tempted to leap, and call it faith? Where are you being asked simply to keep walking the road, trusting the one who guards it?

passages.t: ‘I will be with him in trouble’: God has the last word
passages.happening:
In the last three verses God himself speaks. “Because he loves Me, I will deliver him; because he knows My name, I will protect him” (verse 14).

“When he calls out to Me, I will answer him; I will be with him in trouble. I will deliver him and honor him” (verse 15).

“With long life I will satisfy him and show him My salvation” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The promises now rest on love and knowledge. ‘He loves Me’, ‘he knows My name’. To know God's name in the Psalms is to trust him: “Those who know Your name trust in You” (Psalm 9:10).

Look closely at verse 15. God does not say the one who loves him will never be in trouble. He says, ‘I will be with him in trouble’. The trouble is inside the promise.

Long life was the gift every Israelite hoped for, and the psalm promises it. But its very last word is God's salvation.
passages.later:
At the cross, the chief priests mocked Jesus with words close to this psalm: “He trusts in God. Let God deliver Him now if He wants Him” (Matthew 27:43). God did not deliver him from the cross. Christians believe that on the third day God kept the promise of verse 15 to him, ‘I will deliver him and honor him’, by raising him from the dead.

Jesus said, “Behold, I have given you authority to tread on snakes and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10:19), much as verse 13 speaks.
passages.asks:
Psalm 91 ends with a promise of presence: ‘I will be with him in trouble.’ That is the promise you can hold in any danger, whatever the outcome.

Call on God today (verse 15). Tell him what you fear. Pray for protection, and ask plainly. Then leave the outcome with him, as Jesus did in the garden, and keep using every good gift of care he has given.
